items.name: HiRISE telescopic camera
items.note: Best surface detail. Heavy, power-hungry and makes a lot of data.
specs: about 30 cm per pixel from 300 km

items.name: CRISM imaging spectrometer
items.note: Finds water-related minerals. Moderate power and data.

items.name: SHARAD shallow radar
items.note: Sees layers under the surface. Draws steady power.

items.name: CTX context camera
items.note: Wide views at lower detail. Light and cheap.

items.name: MCS climate sounder
items.note: Profiles the atmosphere. Very little data.
specs: yoke that scans limb and surface

items.name: MARCI colour imager
items.note: Daily weather maps. Small science gain.

items.name: 12 m² Solar Array
items.note: Light and cheap, but little power this far from the Sun.

items.name: 20 m² Solar Array
items.note: Same area as the real orbiter. Balanced.

items.name: 28 m² Solar Array
items.note: Most power and margin. Adds mass and cost.

items.name: 2 m High-Gain Antenna
items.note: Lighter, but sends less data home.

items.name: 3 m High-Gain Antenna
items.note: Same size as the real orbiter. Full downlink.

items.name: Nickel-Hydrogen Battery
items.note: Keeps the craft alive when Mars blocks the Sun.

items.name: Electronics Shielding
items.note: Protects the computer from solar-storm bit flips.

items.name: LROC camera system
items.note: Two narrow-angle cameras and a wide-angle camera: the sharpest maps of landing sites.

items.name: LOLA laser altimeter
items.note: Maps heights and slopes for safe landings.

items.name: Diviner radiometer
items.note: Measures surface temperature, day and night.

items.name: LAMP ultraviolet spectrograph
items.note: Looks for frost in shadowed craters using starlight.

items.name: LEND neutron detector
items.note: Senses hydrogen that may mean water ice. Heavy, little data.
specs: hydrogen, a sign of water ice

items.name: CRaTER radiation telescope
items.note: Measures the radiation future astronauts would face.

items.name: 8 m² Solar Array
items.note: Light and cheap. Full sunlight at the Moon helps.

items.name: 11 m² Solar Array
items.note: Balanced power for a lunar orbiter.

items.name: 15 m² Solar Array
items.note: Most power and margin. Adds mass and cost.

items.name: S-band Antenna
items.note: Simple and light, but slow.

items.name: Ka-band High-Gain Antenna
items.note: Fast downlink, like the real orbiter’s Ka band.

items.name: Battery
items.note: Keeps the craft alive behind the Moon.

items.name: Electronics Shielding
items.note: Protects the computer from solar-storm bit flips.

items.name: Europa Imaging System (EIS)
items.note: Wide and narrow cameras for color and stereo images.
specs: approximate: NASA lists 352 kg for all nine instruments together

items.name: Mapping Imaging Spectrometer (MISE)
items.note: Maps ices, salts and organics on the surface.
specs: approximate: NASA lists 352 kg for all nine instruments together

items.name: Ice-Penetrating Radar (REASON)
items.note: Looks through the ice shell for the ocean below.
specs: approximate: NASA lists 352 kg for all nine instruments together

items.name: Thermal Imager (E-THEMIS)
items.note: Finds warm spots where water may be near the surface.
specs: approximate: NASA lists 352 kg for all nine instruments together

items.name: Magnetometer (ECM)
items.note: Confirms the ocean through Europa’s induced magnetic field.
specs: approximate: NASA lists 352 kg for all nine instruments together

items.name: Mass Spectrometer (MASPEX)
items.note: Analyzes gases in the thin atmosphere and possible plumes.
specs: approximate: NASA lists 352 kg for all nine instruments together

items.name: 80 m² Solar Array
items.note: Lighter, but sunlight at Jupiter is only about 4% of Earth’s.

items.name: 102 m² Solar Array
items.note: Same area as the real arrays.

items.name: 120 m² Solar Array
items.note: More margin, more mass and cost.

items.name: 2 m High-Gain Antenna
items.note: Lighter, but sends less data home.

items.name: 3 m High-Gain Antenna
items.note: Same size as the real dish.

items.name: Battery
items.note: Keeps the craft alive in Jupiter’s shadow.

items.name: Radiation Vault
items.note: Shields the electronics from Jupiter’s radiation belts.

items.name: SEIS seismometer
items.note: Listens for marsquakes to map the planet’s interior.
specs: on the ground by the arm, under a wind shield

items.name: HP3 heat-flow probe
items.note: Hammers into the ground to measure heat escaping from inside Mars.

items.name: RISE radio science
items.note: Tracks the radio signal to measure how Mars wobbles.
specs: the X-band radio and two medium-gain antennas
78 W for up to one hour a day (about 3.3 W on average)

items.name: Robotic arm and cameras
items.note: Places instruments on the ground and images the site.
specs: places SEIS and HP3 on the ground

items.name: Weather sensors (TWINS)
items.note: Measures wind and temperature, so quakes can be told apart from wind.

items.name: Magnetometer
items.note: Measures the magnetic field at the surface.
specs: the magnetic field at the surface

items.name: Round Solar Arrays, 1.8 m
items.note: Light, but dust can leave too little power.

items.name: Round Solar Arrays, 2.15 m
items.note: The same size as InSight’s two arrays.

items.name: Round Solar Arrays, 2.5 m
items.note: More margin for dusty days. Heavier.

items.name: UHF Relay Antenna
items.note: Sends data up to orbiters passing overhead. Light, but slower.

items.name: X-band and UHF Antennas
items.note: Talks to Earth directly and through orbiters.

items.name: Lithium-ion Battery
items.note: Keeps the lander alive through the cold Martian night.

items.name: Light Heat Shield
items.note: Lighter and cheaper, but it can only protect a lighter spacecraft.

items.name: Thick Heat Shield
items.note: Thicker, like InSight’s. Protects a heavier spacecraft.

items.name: Small Parachute
items.note: Lighter, but the engines must do more of the braking.

items.name: Large Parachute
items.note: Slows the lander more, so less descent propellant is needed.

items.name: Mini-RF imaging radar
items.note: A synthetic-aperture radar that looks for ice in shadowed craters.
specs: ice and rough ground in polar craters

items.name: Ultraviolet spectrograph (Europa-UVS)
items.note: Looks for plumes and gases above the surface in ultraviolet light.
specs: approximate: NASA lists 352 kg for all nine instruments together

items.name: Plasma instrument (PIMS)
items.note: Measures the charged particles around Europa so the magnetometer can see the ocean.
specs: approximate: NASA lists 352 kg for all nine instruments together

items.name: Dust analyzer (SUDA)
items.note: Catches tiny grains thrown off Europa and tells what they are made of.
specs: approximate: NASA lists 352 kg for all nine instruments together

items.note: Burns two propellants instead of one. More efficient than hydrazine thrusters, so you need less propellant, but it adds mass and cost.
specs: about 315 s (game value) vs 223 s hydrazine

mars.instrument: The real orbiter carried 139 kg of science instruments in total (JPL MRO press kit). Per-instrument values here are approximate game values.
mars.array: The real orbiter had two arrays, 20 m² in total, giving about 2,000 W at Mars (JPL MRO press kit). Other sizes are game options.
mars.antenna: The real high-gain antenna was a 3 m dish (JPL MRO press kit). The 2 m option is a game option.
mars.battery: The real orbiter used nickel-hydrogen batteries for periods without sunlight (JPL MRO press kit).
mars.shield: Solar storms can flip memory bits and force a safe mode (NASA Earthdata). Mass here is approximate.
mars.engine: Without an engine upgrade the spacecraft uses its built-in hydrazine thrusters (specific impulse 223 s, NTRS 19970010493; LRO’s effective value was 212.2 s, NASA GSFC LRO paper). The bipropellant figures are game values.

moon.instrument: The real orbiter carried about 92 kg of science payload (NASA NSSDC). Per-instrument values here are approximate game values; names say "-style" because the numbers are not the real instruments’.
moon.array: Array sizes here are game options; a NASA figure for the real array was not found.
moon.antenna: The real orbiter sent data in Ka band at up to 100 Mbps (NTRS 20180000056).
moon.battery: Every lunar orbiter passes behind the Moon and needs stored energy. Mass is approximate.
moon.shield: Solar storms can flip memory bits and force a safe mode (NASA Earthdata). Mass is approximate.
moon.engine: Without an engine upgrade the spacecraft uses its built-in hydrazine thrusters (specific impulse 223 s, NTRS 19970010493; LRO’s effective value was 212.2 s, NASA GSFC LRO paper). The bipropellant figures are game values.

europa.instrument: Europa Clipper carries nine instruments, including EIS, MISE, REASON, E-THEMIS, ECM and MASPEX (NASA Science, Europa Clipper instruments). Mass, power and data values are approximate game values.
europa.array: The real arrays total about 102 m² and give at least 700 W at Jupiter (JPL Europa Clipper spacecraft page).
europa.antenna: The real high-gain antenna is a 3 m dish, with seven smaller antennas as backup (JPL Europa Clipper pages).
europa.battery: Jupiter’s shadow cuts sunlight; mass is approximate.
europa.shield: The real vault has aluminum-zinc walls up to 9.2 mm thick to protect the electronics (JPL Europa Clipper quick facts). Mass is approximate.
europa.engine: Without an engine upgrade the spacecraft uses its built-in hydrazine thrusters (specific impulse 223 s, NTRS 19970010493; LRO’s effective value was 212.2 s, NASA GSFC LRO paper). The bipropellant figures are game values.

lander.instrument: InSight carried a seismometer (SEIS), a heat-flow probe (HP3), radio science (RISE), a robotic arm with cameras, and weather sensors (JPL InSight press kit). Mass, power and data values here are approximate game values.
lander.array: InSight’s two round arrays, each about 2.15 m across, give about 600–700 W on a clear day and 200–300 W when dusty (JPL InSight press kit).
lander.antenna: InSight talked to Earth directly and relayed data through orbiters. Values here are game values.
lander.battery: InSight used lithium-ion batteries (JPL InSight press kit). Mass is approximate.
lander.aeroshell: InSight’s aeroshell was 2.64 m across, and its heat shield was slightly thicker than Phoenix’s (JPL InSight press kit). Masses and limits are game values.
lander.parachute: Parachutes slow a lander in the thin Martian air before the engines take over. Masses and savings are game values.
lander.engine: Without an engine upgrade the spacecraft uses its built-in hydrazine thrusters (specific impulse 223 s, NTRS 19970010493; LRO’s effective value was 212.2 s, NASA GSFC LRO paper). The bipropellant figures are game values.
